CONTRACTS REGARDING WILLS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Pat Morgan

PROPOSED CLAIMANT — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION REGARDING A CONTRACT CONCERNING A WILL OR DEVISE
I, Jordan Alex Lee, assert a claim arising from a promise or agreement made with Pat Morgan, who died on June 1, 2026. My relationship to Pat Morgan is: Stepchild. The promise or agreement I am relying on is dated (or was made on or about): March 15, 2010. The property or interest I claim Pat Morgan promised or agreed to leave to me, or not to revoke a provision leaving to me, is described as follows: The decedent's residence at 123 Oak Street, promised in exchange for the claimant providing years of unpaid in-home caregiving. This declaration relates to a proceeding that would be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of Alameda County, under Probate Code § 21700 and Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual pleading asserting a claim to distribution based on a contract concerning a will, devise, or other instrument. It is not itself a court filing, a will, a trust, or a binding contract, and signing it does not establish that any contract existed, that Pat Morgan made any such promise or agreement, or that Jordan Alex Lee is entitled to any distribution — only a court, applying Probate Code § 21700's methods of proof to the actual facts, can determine that.

A CONTRACT CONCERNING A WILL CAN BE PROVEN ONLY IN THE WAYS THE STATUTE LISTS
Probate Code § 21700(a) governs a contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, a contract not to revoke a will or devise or other instrument, or a contract to die intestate, when the contract was made after the statute's effective date. Such a contract regarding Pat Morgan's testamentary plan or intestate succession can be established only by one of five methods the statute lists in § 21700(a)(1)-(5); no other form of proof will do, however persuasive it might otherwise seem.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, or not to revoke a will or devise or other instrument, or to die intestate, if made after the effective date of this statute, can be established only by one of the following:"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21700(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21700.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule for proving a contract concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific decedent's estate, or about whether a particular claimant's facts satisfy any of the five listed methods. The word 'only' in § 21700(a) makes this list exclusive on its face, but this clause does not resolve how a court treats evidence that falls just short of one category (for example, an unsigned draft, or a witness's uncorroborated account of a decedent's oral statement) — the statute's text does not itself define an evidentiary sufficiency threshold below the five listed methods, and this document does not supply one. This document is informational: it does not itself establish, or determine the existence of, any contract concerning a decedent's will, devise, or intestate succession — only a court can do that.

THREE DOCUMENT-BASED WAYS TO PROVE A CONTRACT CONCERNING A WILL
Of the five methods Probate Code § 21700(a) allows, the first three are document-based: (1) the material provisions of the contract are stated directly in a will or other instrument; (2) a will or other instrument expressly refers to a contract, and extrinsic evidence proves the contract's terms; or (3) a writing signed by Pat Morgan evidences the contract, even if that writing is not itself a will or a reference within one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) Provisions of a will or other instrument stating the material provisions of the contract. (2) An expressed reference in a will or other instrument to a contract and extrinsic evidence proving the terms of the contract. (3) A writing signed by the decedent evidencing the contract."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21700(a)(1)-(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21700.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule for proving a contract concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific estate, or about whether any specific document a claimant holds qualifies under (1), (2), or (3). § 21700(a)(2)'s 'extrinsic evidence proving the terms of the contract' and § 21700(a)(3)'s 'writing signed by the decedent evidencing the contract' are not further defined within this section — the statute does not state, for example, how complete a signed writing must be to 'evidence' a contract, or what quantum of extrinsic evidence 'proves' a contract's terms under (2). This document does not resolve those undefined terms for any specific writing. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any writing or will provision satisfies (1), (2), or (3) — only a court can do that.

TWO WAYS TO PROVE A CONTRACT WITHOUT ANY WRITING, BY CLEAR AND CONVINCING EVIDENCE
Probate Code § 21700(a)(4) and (a)(5) allow a contract concerning Pat Morgan's will, devise, or other instrument to be proven without any writing at all, but only by clear and convincing evidence: (4) an agreement between Pat Morgan and Jordan Alex Lee, or a promise by Pat Morgan to Jordan Alex Lee, that is enforceable in equity; or (5) an agreement between Pat Morgan and a third person for Jordan Alex Lee's benefit, or a promise by Pat Morgan to a third person for Jordan Alex Lee's benefit, that is enforceable in equity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(4) Clear and convincing evidence of an agreement between the decedent and the claimant or a promise by the decedent to the claimant that is enforceable in equity. (5) Clear and convincing evidence of an agreement between the decedent and another person for the benefit of the claimant or a promise by the decedent to another person for the benefit of the claimant that is enforceable in equity."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(a)(4)-(5) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21700(a)(4)-(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21700.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule for proving a contract concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific estate, or about whether any specific account of an agreement or promise meets the clear-and-convincing standard. § 21700 uses the phrase 'clear and convincing evidence' but does not itself define that evidentiary standard, define what makes a promise 'enforceable in equity,' or list the elements of an enforceable-in-equity promise (such as reliance or part performance); this document has not independently fetched or verified the text of whatever Evidence Code or case-law source defines those terms, and does not supply that definition here. This document is informational: it does not itself weigh evidence or determine that any agreement or promise meets this standard — only a court can do that.

SIGNING A JOINT OR MUTUAL WILL DOES NOT, BY ITSELF, PROVE A CONTRACT NOT TO REVOKE IT
Probate Code § 21700(b) provides that the mere execution of a joint will, or of mutual wills, does not create a presumption of a contract not to revoke the will or wills. If two people — for example, Pat Morgan and another testator — sign a joint will or mirror-image mutual wills, that fact alone does not shift any burden toward finding a binding contract between them; a contract not to revoke still has to be established under one of the five methods listed in § 21700(a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The execution of a joint will or mutual wills does not create a presumption of a contract not to revoke the will or wills."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21700(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21700.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule on joint and mutual wills — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific pair of wills, or about whether any specific joint or mutual will happens to also satisfy one of § 21700(a)'s five methods (for example, by stating the contract's material provisions within the will itself, which would independently satisfy (a)(1)). § 21700(b) does not itself define 'joint will' or 'mutual wills'; this document does not supply definitions for those terms beyond the statute's own text. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether any specific joint or mutual will was, or was not, made under a binding contract not to revoke — only a court can do that.

CONTRACTS MADE BEFORE JANUARY 1, 2001 ARE GOVERNED BY THE PRIOR LAW, NOT THIS STATUTE'S LIST
Probate Code § 21700(c) carves out contracts made before the statute's effective date: a contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, not to revoke one, or to die intestate, if made before § 21700 took effect, is construed under whatever law applied to that contract before § 21700's effective date — not under the five-method list in § 21700(a). The statute's own enactment history states it was added effective January 1, 2001.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, or not to revoke a will or devise or other instrument, or to die intestate, if made prior to the effective date of this section, shall be construed under the law applicable to the contract prior to the effective date of this section."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21700(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21700.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's transition rule for pre-existing contracts concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific older contract, or about what the substantive 'law applicable to the contract' before January 1, 2001 actually required. § 21700(c) does not itself restate that prior law; determining it would require researching pre-2001 case law and any predecessor statute, which this document has not done — a CourtListener case-law search for this topic was attempted separately and is disclosed in a companion clause. This document is informational: it does not itself determine which body of law governs any specific pre-2001 contract, or resolve any dispute over one — only a court can do that.

A CLAIM TO DISTRIBUTION BASED ON A PROMISE OR AGREEMENT MUST BE BROUGHT WITHIN ONE YEAR OF DEATH
Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3(a) sets a special filing deadline for a claim like Jordan Alex Lee's: if a person has a claim that arises from a promise or agreement with a decedent — such as Pat Morgan — to distribution from an estate or trust or under another instrument, whether that promise or agreement was oral or in writing, an action to enforce the claim to distribution may be commenced within one year after the date of death. That one-year period replaces whatever limitations period would otherwise have applied to the underlying promise or agreement (for example, the limitations period that would normally apply to a written or oral contract claim).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If a person has a claim that arises from a promise or agreement with a decedent to distribution from an estate or trust or under another instrument, whether the promise or agreement was made orally or in writing, an action to enforce the claim to distribution may be commenced within one year after the date of death, and the limitations period that would have been applicable does not apply."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 366.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 366.3(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=366.3.)

This document is informational: it does not itself calculate any deadline or determine whether any specific claim is timely — only a court, applying this statute to the actual filing date, can do that.

THE ONE-YEAR DEADLINE IS NOT TOLLED OR EXTENDED, EXCEPT BY TWO NARROW STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS
Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3(b) makes the one-year filing period in § 366.3(a) essentially rigid: it may not be tolled or extended for any reason, except as provided in Code of Civil Procedure §§ 12, 12a, and 12b, and except as provided in former Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with § 21300) of Division 11, as that former part read before its repeal by Chapter 174 of the Statutes of 2008.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The limitations period provided in this section for commencement of an action shall not be tolled or extended for any reason except as provided in Sections 12, 12a, and 12b of this code, and former Part 3 (commencing with Section 21300) of Division 11 of the Probate Code, as that part read prior to its repeal by Chapter 174 of the Statutes of 2008."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 366.3(b) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 366.3(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=366.3.)

This document has not independently fetched or verified the text of CCP §§ 12, 12a, or 12b (which govern how deadlines falling on weekends, holidays, or court-closure days are computed), or the text of former Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with § 21300) as it read before its 2008 repeal; this clause relies only on § 366.3(b)'s own cross-reference to those provisions, not on their substance. This document is informational: it does not itself toll, extend, or compute any deadline for any specific claim — only a court, applying these cross-referenced provisions, can do that.

THE ONE-YEAR DEADLINE APPLIES ONLY TO DEATHS ON OR AFTER THE STATUTE'S EFFECTIVE DATE
Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3(c) limits the one-year filing rule in § 366.3(a)-(b) to actions brought on claims concerning persons who died on or after this section's effective date. The version of § 366.3 quoted in this document's companion clauses carries a legislative history note that it was amended effective January 1, 2010.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section applies to actions brought on claims concerning persons dying on or after the effective date of this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 366.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 366.3(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=366.3.)
  "Amended by Stats. 2009, Ch. 348, Sec. 3."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 366.3, legislative history note (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 366.3, hist. note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=366.3.)

This document is informational: it does not itself determine which version of this statute governs any specific decedent's estate — only a court can do that.

SUMMARY OF THE EVIDENCE A CLAIMANT BELIEVES SUPPORTS A CONTRACT CONCERNING A WILL
Regarding the promise or agreement described above between Jordan Alex Lee and Pat Morgan, dated on or about March 15, 2010: the evidence I believe supports this claim, and the Probate Code § 21700(a) category or categories I believe it falls under, is described as follows: The decedent's residence at 123 Oak Street, promised in exchange for the claimant providing years of unpaid in-home caregiving. This summary is a personal account for Jordan Alex Lee's own records and for discussion with counsel; it is not a sworn declaration filed with any court, is not itself a will, instrument, or signed writing under § 21700(a)(1)-(3), and does not itself establish that clear and convincing evidence exists under § 21700(a)(4)-(5). Whether this account, together with any documents it references, actually satisfies one of § 21700(a)'s five methods is a determination only a court can make.

Whether this account, together with any documents it references, actually satisfies one of § 21700(a)'s five methods is a determination only a court can make.

I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 6, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside actual pleadings, if any, asserting a claim to distribution from the estate of Pat Morgan based on a contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, not to revoke one, or to die intestate, filed with the California superior court for the administration of that estate. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete such a pleading, and it does not establish any contract, extend or compute any filing deadline, or determine that any claim is timely under Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3 — only a court can do that.]
